query_text: Why do things far away in the distance like hills have a blue hue?

content.text:
Distant hills often look **blue** because of the way Earth’s atmosphere scatters sunlight.

Sunlight contains many colors. Shorter wavelengths—especially **blue and violet**—scatter more easily off tiny air molecules and particles than longer wavelengths like red or orange. This is called **Rayleigh scattering**, the same basic reason the sky looks blue.

When you look at a faraway hill, you’re not just seeing light reflected from the hill. You’re also looking through a lot of air between you and it. That air scatters blue light from the sky into your line of sight, adding a bluish “veil” over the distant object. The farther away the hill is, the more atmosphere you’re looking through, so the stronger the blue tint becomes.

Also, distant objects look paler and lower-contrast because particles, moisture, and haze scatter light and wash out detail. Artists call this effect **atmospheric perspective** or **aerial perspective**.

So in short: **faraway hills look blue because the air between you and them scatters blue sky-light into your eyes and reduces the contrast of the hills themselves.**
